about: Consolidation, Integration and Feedback Week B (MBBS0021) is the second of three review weeks in UCL's MBBS Year 1. In 2026–27 it falls in the week beginning 8 February 2027 (Term 2), straight after Circulation and Breathing. Like the other CIF weeks it is there to consolidate and integrate the preceding modules and give feedback; UCL's 2026–27 Year 1 assessment guide says the February formative is an online paper combining knowledge and practical content, taken as a mock examination under exam conditions and using the same SBA and VSA question types as the summative Applied Knowledge Tests. This guide explains the week and how to prepare; it does not invent a syllabus.

notes.h: What CIF Week B is and where it fits
notes.body:
Consolidation, Integration and Feedback Week B (MBBS0021) is not a taught subject with its own syllabus. It is the second of the three review weeks in UCL's MBBS Year 1, listed on UCL's Year 1 programme page alongside CIF Weeks A (MBBS0020) and C (MBBS0022).

Where it sits in 2026–27
- UCL's 2026–27 overall timetable places CIF B in the week beginning 8 February 2027 (Term 2).
- It comes straight after Circulation and Breathing, which runs from December 2026 to early February 2027 with the winter break in the middle, and just before Fluids, Nutrition and Metabolism begins.
- So by CIF B you will have covered Foundations of Health and Medical Practice, Infection and Defence and Circulation and Breathing, alongside the Clinical and Professional Practice strands that run through the year.
- Dates move from year to year, so check the current timetable on Moodle.

What the week is for
- Like the other CIF weeks, it exists to consolidate and integrate the preceding modules and to give you feedback on your progress.
- What makes CIF B different is the mock exam. UCL's 2026–27 Year 1 Format of Assessments document says the February formative assessment is taken as a mock examination under exam conditions (see the next note).

Background from an older guide
- UCL's Year 1 Study Guide from 2018–19 described CIF weeks as a mix of case-based and lecture-theatre sessions designed to revise the preceding module, link it to the other modules and strands, and provide formative assessment, feedback and a meeting with your personal tutor (it mentioned the tutor meeting for CIF A and CIF B).
- It also said the February formative assessments covered all modules taught so far, not just the most recent one.
- That guide is several years old and the assessment formats have changed since, so treat it as background only and rely on current Moodle information.

Why it matters even though it is formative
- Formative means the mark does not count towards progression. But a mock run under exam conditions is the closest rehearsal you will get for the end-of-year Applied Knowledge Tests, and it tests material from across the first half of the year.

Exam tips: treat CIF B as the real thing. Revise all three systems modules before the week, not only Circulation and Breathing, and sit the mock without notes so the feedback shows where you really are.

notes.h: The February mock: an online paper under exam conditions
notes.body:
UCL's 2026–27 Year 1 Format of Assessments document describes the formative assessments held in the CIF weeks. For February it says:
- The assessment is online and integrated: knowledge and practical testing are combined in a single question paper.
- It is taken as a mock examination under exam conditions.
- Its stated purposes are to encourage efficient learning and to let you experience all the question types used in the end-of-year summative assessments.

The two question types
- Single Best Answer (SBA): a stem (often a clinical scenario), a lead-in question and five options. More than one option may be partly right; you choose the best. Technique: read the lead-in first, try to answer before looking at the options, then eliminate options that are wrong or less specific. Watch qualifiers such as 'most likely', 'first' and 'most appropriate'.
- Very Short Answer (VSA): you type your own answer of no more than five words. There is no list to recognise the answer from, so it tests true recall. Give one specific term and spell it accurately; do not offer two answers.
- Practical content (for example anatomy, histology or data interpretation) sits within the same online paper, so images can appear in either type.

How the mock relates to the summative AKTs
- The same document describes the end-of-year summative assessment as two Applied Knowledge Test papers, each a two-hour online paper worth no more than 100 marks, mixing SBA and VSA questions that may include images, with no negative marking.
- It says the assessments are blueprinted to the year of study, the UCL Curriculum Map and the GMC's Good medical practice and Outcomes for graduates, and integrate across modules and disciplines, including Clinical and Professional Practice teaching.
- The document does not give the length or number of questions in the February mock, so check Moodle (UCL points students to sample questions on the Assessment Unit Moodle site).

Exam conditions: what that means for you
- Sit it in one go, without notes, without discussing questions, and within the time allowed. If you look things up during the mock, the feedback stops being useful.
- Practise pacing. In the summative papers, two hours for up to 100 marks gives a little over a minute per mark (120 ÷ 100 = 1.2 minutes), so you cannot get stuck on one hard question.
- Because there is no negative marking in the summative papers, never leave an answer blank there; make your best attempt and flag the question to revisit.

Exam tips: do at least two timed practice blocks of mixed SBA questions in the week before CIF B, and practise VSA recall by covering the options of SBA questions.

notes.h: Preparing for the week and using your feedback
notes.body:
CIF B is most useful when you prepare properly and then act on the results.

Before the week
- Revise across all the modules so far, not only Circulation and Breathing. The 2018–19 Study Guide said February formatives covered all modules to date; whatever this year's exact coverage, the summative AKTs will integrate across the whole year.
- Use the learning objectives on Moodle for each module as your checklist. Mark each one as secure, shaky or not yet learned.
- Revise actively: practice questions, flashcards, drawing diagrams from memory (cardiac cycle, oxygen dissociation curve, immune responses) and explaining topics aloud. Rereading notes feels productive but is less effective.
- Integrate: for each topic, ask how it links to anatomy and imaging, pathology, use of medicines, data and statistics, and communication and ethics. For example, pneumonia links infection and immune defence with gas exchange, oxygen therapy and antibiotic principles.
- Look after the basics: sleep, food and breaks. A mock is not worth exhausting yourself for.

After the mock: making sense of your results
- Go through every question you got wrong and every one you guessed right. For each, decide why: a knowledge gap, a misread question, poor technique (such as not reading the lead-in), or running out of time.
- Look for patterns. Are your errors clustered in one module, one discipline (for example anatomy or pharmacology), or one question type (VSA spelling, data interpretation)?
- Turn the patterns into a short action plan with dates, and fit it around Fluids, Nutrition and Metabolism, which starts straight afterwards.
- Revisit weak topics after a gap (spaced repetition) rather than once immediately.

Getting support
- Your personal tutor is the first person to talk to about academic progress. The 2018–19 guide described a scheduled tutor meeting around CIF A and CIF B; check whether that is still the arrangement.
- UCL Medical School has a student support team, and UCL has wider well-being services, if problems outside your studies are affecting your work.

Looking ahead
- CIF C, in late April or early May, is the last review week before the end-of-year assessments. What you fix after CIF B gives you time to consolidate before then.

Exam tips: a low mock score with a clear action plan is more useful than a high score you cannot explain. Write your plan within a few days, while the questions are fresh.

notes.h: Practice questions in the SBA and VSA styles
notes.body:
The questions in this section practise UCL's formats (five-option SBA, and short recall answers like VSAs) using standard basic-science content of the kind covered in the first half of Year 1. They are not taken from UCL papers, and UCL does not publish the content of the February mock, so use the Moodle learning objectives to check coverage.

How to use them
- Read the lead-in, cover the options and answer first; then choose from the options.
- For VSA-style items, write no more than five words and check spelling.
- Read the explanations even when you are right: each distractor is built on a common mistake.

Core ideas these questions draw on
- Breathing: the diaphragm is the main muscle of quiet inspiration and is supplied by the phrenic nerve (roots C3–C5). Accessory muscles, such as sternocleidomastoid (accessory nerve), help in forced breathing.
- Cardiac output: stroke volume = end-diastolic volume − end-systolic volume; ejection fraction = stroke volume ÷ end-diastolic volume. With EDV 120 mL and ESV 50 mL, SV is 70 mL and ejection fraction is about 58% (typical approximate values).
- Blood pressure control: on standing, blood pools in the legs and arterial pressure falls; baroreceptors in the carotid sinus and aortic arch fire less, so sympathetic outflow rises and vagal outflow falls within seconds. Hormonal responses (renin–angiotensin–aldosterone, ADH) act more slowly.
- Carbon dioxide transport: carbonic anhydrase in red cells converts CO₂ and water to carbonic acid, which dissociates to H⁺ and bicarbonate; most CO₂ travels as bicarbonate.
- Heart anatomy: the mitral valve lies between the left atrium and left ventricle; the tricuspid valve between the right atrium and right ventricle.

Exam tips: after each practice block, write one line on why you missed each wrong answer. Those lines become your revision list.

questions.q: Which nerve provides the motor supply to the diaphragm, the main muscle of quiet inspiration?
questions.why: The phrenic nerve (C3–C5) is the motor nerve to the diaphragm. The vagus nerve carries parasympathetic and sensory fibres to the thoracic and abdominal organs but does not move the diaphragm. The intercostal nerves supply the intercostal muscles, which help raise the ribs, so they are a common confusion. The accessory nerve supplies sternocleidomastoid and trapezius, which act as accessory muscles in forced breathing. The long thoracic nerve supplies serratus anterior.

questions.q: A healthy adult's left ventricle has an end-diastolic volume of 120 mL and an end-systolic volume of 50 mL. What is the ejection fraction?
questions.why: Stroke volume = 120 − 50 = 70 mL, and ejection fraction = 70 ÷ 120 ≈ 58%. About 42% is end-systolic ÷ end-diastolic volume, which is the fraction left behind, not the fraction ejected. 70% treats the stroke volume in millilitres as if it were a percentage. 140% divides stroke volume by end-systolic volume instead of end-diastolic volume. 240% divides end-diastolic by end-systolic volume.

questions.q: A 19-year-old stands up quickly after lying down. Which change happens within the first few seconds to restore arterial pressure?
options: Increased firing of the carotid sinus baroreceptors
Increased vagal outflow to the heart
A fall in total peripheral resistance
Increased secretion of antidiuretic hormone as the main corrective response
Increased sympathetic outflow, raising heart rate and peripheral resistance
questions.why: Standing pools blood in the legs, arterial pressure falls and the baroreceptors are stretched less, so the medulla increases sympathetic outflow, raising heart rate, contractility and peripheral resistance. Baroreceptor firing falls rather than rises when pressure drops, so increased firing has the direction reversed. Increased vagal outflow would slow the heart and lower pressure further; vagal outflow is reduced. A fall in peripheral resistance would also lower pressure; arterioles constrict instead. ADH and the renin–angiotensin system do help, but they act over minutes to hours, so they are not the main response in the first seconds.

questions.q: Explain how sitting the February CIF mock 'under exam conditions' makes its feedback more useful, and give two ways to act on that feedback.
markScheme: Exam conditions (timed, no notes, no conferring) mean the score reflects genuine recall and pacing, as in the summative AKTs
Gives realistic experience of SBA and VSA formats and timing across integrated content
Action: classify each error (knowledge gap, misreading, technique, timing) and look for patterns by module/discipline/question type
Action: make a dated revision plan with spaced review; discuss progress with personal tutor if concerned
questions.modelAnswer: Sitting the mock under exam conditions, timed and without notes or discussion, means the result reflects what you can actually recall and how well you manage time, which is what the summative Applied Knowledge Tests will test. It also gives realistic practice of the SBA and VSA formats on integrated content. To act on it, first go through every wrong or guessed answer and classify the cause (a knowledge gap, misreading the question, poor technique or running out of time), looking for patterns by module, discipline or question type. Then turn those patterns into a dated revision plan using spaced review, and talk to your personal tutor if the results worry you.
